task_row_model.query: For a patient over 50 with suspected giant cell arteritis presenting with new temporal headache, jaw claudication, and an elevated ESR but no vision loss, what is the recommended initial management? Specifically, when should glucocorticoids be started relative to temporal artery biopsy, what dosing is appropriate (including when to use IV steroids), and what is the acceptable timing for biopsy and adjunctive diagnostic tests?

documents.content: Temporal artery biopsy remains a diagnostic standard for suspected large-vessel vasculitis. The procedure typically yields a 1–2 cm segment of artery; longer specimens and sampling from both sides increase diagnostic sensitivity because of skip lesions. Histopathology classically shows transmural granulomatous inflammation with disruption of the internal elastic lamina and multinucleated giant cells, although giant cells are absent in a minority of positive cases. Proper handling includes prompt fixation and communication with pathology to examine multiple levels. Imaging such as ultrasound can guide targeted biopsy sites but biopsy technique itself focuses on obtaining adequate length and avoiding crush artifact.

documents.content: Peripheral arterial disease in the lower extremities commonly presents with exertional claudication. Diagnosis relies on history, physical exam, and ankle-brachial index measurement; values below 0.90 suggest occlusive disease. Initial noninvasive management emphasizes supervised exercise therapy and smoking cessation. Pharmacologic therapy includes antiplatelet agents and cilostazol to improve walking distance; statin therapy and risk factor control are essential. Revascularization with endovascular angioplasty or surgical bypass is considered for lifestyle-limiting symptoms refractory to conservative measures or for critical limb ischemia with rest pain or tissue loss.

documents.content: When giant cell arteritis is suspected clinically (age >50, new temporal headache, jaw claudication, raised ESR/CRP), begin high-dose glucocorticoid therapy immediately rather than delaying for diagnostic procedures to prevent irreversible ischemic complications. For patients without visual symptoms, oral prednisone 40–60 mg daily (approximately 1 mg/kg up to ~60 mg) is typical; if there is visual disturbance or threatened vision, give IV methylprednisolone 500–1000 mg daily for 1–3 days before transitioning to oral therapy. Obtain temporal artery biopsy and/or vascular imaging promptly, but do not withhold steroids for biopsy; biopsy is most useful if performed within the first 1–2 weeks after steroid initiation, and diagnostic yield may persist for up to 2–4 weeks.

documents.content: Glucocorticoids are the cornerstone of therapy for suspected giant cell arteritis and related polymyalgia rheumatica. Typical initial oral prednisone dosing ranges from 15–20 mg daily for isolated polymyalgic features to 40–60 mg daily for cranial symptoms. After symptom control for 2–4 weeks, a gradual taper is undertaken guided by symptoms and inflammatory markers; many regimens reduce by 5–10 mg every 2–4 weeks until 20 mg, then more slowly. Preventive measures include calcium and vitamin D, bisphosphonates in high-risk patients, gastric protection as indicated, and monitoring for steroid adverse effects during prolonged therapy.

documents.content: Management of symptomatic carotid artery stenosis focuses on stroke risk reduction. For symptomatic high-grade stenosis (typically >70% by validated duplex/angiography), carotid endarterectomy is often recommended in appropriate surgical candidates; carotid stenting may be considered for selected patients or high surgical risk. Medical therapy includes antiplatelet agents, statin therapy, blood pressure control, and smoking cessation. Preoperative imaging should characterize plaque morphology and percent stenosis. Timing of revascularization after a transient ischemic event balances early stroke risk against perioperative complication rates.
